Beethoven is licensed, not sold: you receive a license to use it under the Trial Edition License Agreement below and the privacy statement, accepted once in a signing dialog on the extension's own setup page. 1. WHAT BEETHOVEN IS

"Beethoven" means the browser extension of that name (the "Extension"), the small helper program that ships inside the Extension for you to install on your computer and that carries the Extension's ssh connection (the "Bridge", which Beethoven's screens call the helper), the scripts and programs that your institution's lab keeps in one shared copy on your institution's cluster, which the Extension points your computing account at, or that an earlier version of the Extension installed in your own computing account (either way, the "Framework"), the recipe for the container image the Framework runs, its documentation, and updates Licensor provides. A pilot edition of the Extension made as an installable web app (the "Pilot App") is given only to a person who asks for it, by their lab lead, as a file; it is not offered on the private listing, it is part of Beethoven while you use it, and it counts as an installation under section 3(e). The Extension starts, watches and stops a job in your own cluster account, over a secure shell ("ssh") connection to your cluster's login node where it can make one (the "ssh path"), and otherwise through your institution's Open OnDemand portal (the "portal path"); the job runs Claude Code, Anthropic's program, which you have signed in to yourself, and makes that session visible to you at claude.ai and in the Claude app through Anthropic's Remote Control feature. "Trial Edition" means the edition this agreement covers: free of charge during the evaluation period, for persons whose institutional account Licensor has approved. "Full Edition" means the paid edition, if Licensor offers one, governed by the separate Beethoven Full Edition License Agreement, which you accept only if you choose that edition. "Your portal" means your institution's Open OnDemand portal, and "your account name" means the name of your account on your institution's cluster as the cluster confirms it when you sign in: on the portal path, the name that portal's dashboard shows for the session you signed in to; on the ssh path, the name you type into Beethoven's own sign-in sheet, once the cluster has accepted the sign-in made with it, or the name the cluster reports for a sign-in made with the key of section 5(b)(iii). It is the only identifier of you that Beethoven uses (the Extension also names its own installation with a random number, section 3(e)). "Named Dependencies" are the outside parties and conditions listed in section 7.

3. APPROVAL AND WITHDRAWAL

(a) The Trial Edition is available only to persons whose institutional account Licensor has approved for it. Approval is requested on the request page at https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/request.html, with your account name and the Google account at which you are to receive the invitation to the Extension's private listing, and may be refused or withdrawn at any time, with or without reason. Licensor may approve an account for membership of its lab only; such an approval does not cover Beethoven. There is no key and no password of Licensor's: your own sign-in to your institution's cluster identifies you. After you have accepted this agreement, and only once your cluster has accepted your sign-in (over the ssh path or the portal path), the Extension asks Licensor's access service whether your account name is approved: when you first sign in after accepting it, about once a day while it is in use, and again when you open its panel after a day has passed or after a no; and it starts a worker only while the answer is yes. A copy of Beethoven used from an account that is not approved does not start a worker; its panel offers a link to ask for access instead.

(b) Your approval is for you and the institutional account it names alone. Do not use Beethoven from an account that is not yours, and do not arrange for anyone else to use it under your approval. Sharing your copy of Beethoven, your installation of it or your account with anyone else is a breach of this agreement.

(c) No payment is taken for the Trial Edition, nothing converts automatically into a paid license, and no charge follows its end. Beethoven contains the code that asks for and enforces approval; you may not disable, remove or work around it.

(d) Licensor may withdraw an approval that has been misused (including one shared with anyone else or used from an installation other than yours), given in error or obtained by misrepresentation, or for any other reason. Once your approval is withdrawn, the Extension stops starting workers at its next check and tells you so. Beethoven also checks its own version against a signed list of withdrawn versions; a withdrawn version stops sending commands and tells you to update.

(e) One installation. Your approval covers one installation of the Extension: one browser profile on one computer. The Extension makes a random installation identifier for itself the first time it needs one (when you accept this agreement), from the browser's random number generator; it is not taken or derived from your computer, its hardware or anything else about you, and it is removed when you uninstall the Extension, so a reinstallation is a new installation. The first installation that asks about your approved account is bound to it. An approval check from any other installation (another computer, another browser profile or a reinstallation) is refused, and the Extension says so, until Licensor moves your approval to that installation; ask your lab lead, or write to the notice address on the support page. Likewise, an installation bound to one approved account serves that account only: a check from it for any other account is refused, and the Extension says so, until Licensor releases it. Licensor may refuse every check from a version of the Extension that sends no installation identifier; the current version is on the private listing. The Bridge you install on the same computer, and the key the Extension keeps in that browser profile (section 5(b)(iii)), belong to that installation and are not installations of their own.

5. WHAT BEETHOVEN DOES WITH YOUR CREDENTIALS AND YOUR WORK

This section describes the software as shipped, so that you can hold Licensor to it.

(a) Claude. Beethoven never reads, stores, copies, prints or relays a Claude credential. You sign in to Claude Code yourself, through Anthropic's own flow, once, in a terminal on a compute node of your own cluster account. The Extension starts that terminal for you, in the same command that starts your worker, through your portal's shell or, on the ssh path, through a connection you signed in to with your cluster password and code (the key of section 5(b)(iii) can never start it), opens Anthropic's sign-in page in a new tab, shows you one box, and closes that tab once Claude Code reports you are signed in, unless the tab has loaded another page since you pasted the code; you sign in on Anthropic's page and paste the one-time code it shows into that box. The Extension types the code once into that terminal and keeps no copy of it: it is not stored, not written to the audit log and not sent to Licensor or anyone else, and the Extension never reads Anthropic's page or your clipboard to obtain it. Claude Code makes its credential from the code and keeps it in its own folder in your cluster account; the Framework only starts Claude Code where that credential already is, and Beethoven reads Claude Code's own report of whether it is signed in, with the account and plan that report names, nothing more. You use one Claude account, your own. You answer Claude Code's one-time question about Remote Control yourself, with the box you tick in the Extension's panel before your first worker starts; the Framework records that answer in one file in your cluster account when you press Connect, and your worker gives it to Claude Code when Claude Code asks. Trust for the worker's own folder is recorded in Claude Code's settings by the Framework when a worker starts. Beethoven gives Claude Code no answer you have not given.

(b) Your sign-in to your cluster. The Extension reaches your cluster in one of two ways and tries the first before the second: the ssh path, which needs no VPN, and the portal path, which may need your institution's VPN (at Wayne State, GlobalProtect). It never signs in to Claude for you on either path (see (a)). The ssh path is new in this version and has been tried only against ssh servers that Licensor ran itself, set up like your institution's, not yet with a real account on a real cluster.

(i) The Bridge. A browser extension cannot open an ssh connection by itself, so the ssh path needs a bridge that carries the Extension's encrypted connection to your cluster's ssh port and back. In this version that is the Bridge: a small helper program that ships inside the Extension, which you install once on your computer, in your own user account and without administrator rights, by saving the installer the Extension offers you from its own package and running it (the Extension cannot run a program for you). Your browser starts the Bridge only when the Extension asks for it, and the Bridge ends when the Extension lets it go. The Bridge opens a network connection only to your cluster's ssh port (at Wayne State, grid.wayne.edu, port 22, and another address only if its installer wrote one into its settings), carries bytes both ways without reading, keeping or logging them, holds no password, key or other credential, offers no shell and runs no other program. The uninstaller placed beside it removes it. The Extension can also carry the ssh path through a relay server, but only one that your institution's site profile names; none is named in this version, and if one ever is, the privacy statement will name who runs it and what it sees before any version uses it. If no Bridge is installed and you do not install one, or your cluster's ssh port cannot be reached from your network, the Extension uses the portal path.

(ii) Your password and code. The first time you use the ssh path in this browser, again whenever the key of (iii) is missing or refused, and when you sign in to Claude on the ssh path (see (a)), the Extension asks you to sign in on its own sign-in sheet, a page of the Extension: your account name, your cluster password and, where your cluster asks for one, the one-time verification code from your authenticator app (at Wayne State, Google Authenticator). The Extension sends them only to your cluster, inside the encrypted ssh connection, after your cluster's identity (its host key) has matched the one the Extension carries for it, and only for that sign-in. It never stores them, never writes them to a log, never offers to remember them, and never sends them to Licensor or anyone else. It never makes a verification code and never holds the secret your authenticator app keeps. If your cluster refuses a code with words that may mean a mistyped code or no verification code set up, the Extension asks you which, and only if you say you have none does it show you your institution's own instructions for setting one up, which you follow yourself, on your institution's pages; Beethoven takes no part in that step. After your first sign-in on the sheet, the Extension keeps that signed-in connection open, in your browser's memory only, for up to ten minutes, so that your first Connect can run the Claude sign-in of (a) in it without asking for your password and code again; it closes when that sign-in ends, when the ten minutes pass, when you cancel, or when your browser closes, and nothing of it is stored.

(iii) The key in your browser. In that sign-in the Extension makes a key in your browser and runs the Framework's browser-key step in your cluster account, which adds one line to your account's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys file. That line lets the key run only the Framework's gate: a fixed list of short commands that report the Framework's version and your account name, start a worker without any Claude sign-in, read your worker's state and its own named files, stop it, mark its workspace restricted, and remove the line itself, within limits on how many workers it may name and how often it may start one. Through that line the key gets no terminal, no other command, no file transfer and no forwarding, and the gate can never sign a worker in to Claude. Later connections from this browser sign in with the key and ask you for nothing. The key's private half never leaves your browser and is never sent to Licensor. By default it is stored encrypted under a second key that your browser keeps and lets no page or script copy out, and Beethoven uses it without asking you; both are stored with the Extension's data in your browser profile on this computer, so someone who can use that browser profile, or read your computer account's files, could use the key, within the limits of that line. If you choose, Beethoven instead keeps the key encrypted under a secret that only your passkey releases (Windows Hello, Touch ID, or your device's PIN or password), so that it cannot be used until you unlock it, once each time you open your browser. That protection is off unless you turn it on, on the sign-in sheet, when Beethoven offers it once after setup, or in Settings, and you can turn it off again in Settings. Turned on later, it protects the key from then on; for a while your browser's own files may still hold the earlier form, until the browser tidies its database, so if you want the protection from the start, choose it on the sign-in sheet. Your lab may set the line to lapse after a number of days, after which the Extension asks you to sign in with your password and code again.

(iv) Forgetting this computer. "Forget this computer", in the Extension's Settings, deletes the key from your browser and asks your cluster, through the gate, to remove its line. If your cluster cannot be reached, or the key is protected and you do not unlock it, the Extension says so, and the line stays until it is removed, which the command "hpcworker browser-key remove", run in a terminal on your cluster, does. The line is what lets the key in: once it is gone from your cluster, a copy of the key left anywhere is of no use. Withdrawing your approval under section 3 does not remove the line; Forget this computer or that command does. In this version your account keeps one such line: signing in over ssh from another browser replaces it, and the key of the browser you used before stops working. Uninstalling the Extension deletes the key from your browser but cannot remove the line from your cluster, so use Forget this computer first. A passkey you made under (iii) is kept by your system or your browser's password manager, not by the Extension: Forget this computer asks it to drop the passkey, and where it does not, you delete it there.

(v) The portal path. The Extension uses the sign-in your browser already holds for your institution's Open OnDemand portal, on that one website only, from its own background and without a portal tab where your browser allows it. It never reads that sign-in, never reads, stores or types a portal password, never signs in for you and never touches a multi-factor step. When the portal asks for a sign-in, the Extension opens the portal in a tab for you to sign in there (in your browser's own sign-in box, or on the portal's own sign-in page), never sees what you type there, and closes that tab once you are signed in, while it is still on the portal. Where your portal does not share its sign-in with the Extension, it keeps that tab behind your other tabs until the work in hand is done and then closes it, and for a later action opens the portal in a background tab and closes it again. The one thing it reads about you from the portal is your account name, from the portal's own dashboard page. If your portal's shell asks for your cluster password, as it may for an account that has no key on the cluster, the Extension types nothing there and offers a one-time step instead: it opens the portal's own terminal page in a tab, and you type your password there yourself; the Extension never sees it. Once you say you are in, or the page's title shows that your shell is up, the Extension types one line into that terminal (or leaves it on your clipboard for you to paste), which runs the Framework's login-setup step in your own account. That step makes a key in your cluster account, in its ~/.ssh folder, that opens your account only from the computer the terminal came from, which at your institution is its Open OnDemand server (it is a file in your own account, protected as your other files are, and hidden from Claude Code inside your worker; anyone who obtained it and could connect from that server could use it), and has ssh offer it when the portal's shell connects you, so that the shell need not ask for your password; it never reads, changes or prints a key you already have. The key stays in your cluster account: the Extension never sees it, keeps nothing about it in your browser and sends nothing about it to Licensor. The command "hpcworker login-setup --remove", run in a terminal on the cluster, removes it. This step has been tried only against the Licensor's mock portal, not yet on a real cluster by an account without a key.

(c) Your account name, as your cluster confirmed it, and the answer of the last approval check with its time are stored in the Extension's own storage in your browser. Nothing about your approval is copied to your cluster account; the Framework has no key, password or account list of Licensor's.

(d) The Framework makes a random token for each job so that only your own browser session can reach your worker. It is kept in a file only you can read, is never shown, and never appears on a command line or in a job log.

(e) Where your work goes. Files the worker reads and every command's output are sent to Anthropic. While you are connected through claude.ai the transcript is also stored on Anthropic's servers. A personal plan is retained five years if model training is on and 30 days otherwise. No BAA covers a personal plan. FERPA records, IRB data and export-controlled technical data must not be in the working directory. Remote Control usage draws from your plan's shared limit. The Extension shows these sentences in short form, with the full text one click away, before your first worker starts, and a one-line reminder beside Connect each time you start one, and does not start a worker in a folder you have marked restricted.

(f) The Extension runs no code on claude.ai or any other Anthropic page and reads nothing from them. It runs no page script on the ssh path. Its only page script runs on the one portal website you connect, on the portal path: where your portal does not share its sign-in with the Extension, to carry the Extension's requests there, and, during the one-time step in (b)(v), on the portal's terminal page, where it watches only the page's title and types only the one line described there. It opens an Anthropic page only in a new tab, as a bookmark would: the sign-in page during the sign-in described in (a), your worker's session page when a worker you started is ready (unless you turn that off) and when you choose "Open my session" or "New session", the connectors settings page if you choose the optional Google Drive step, and the plans page if you follow "See plans" on the welcome page; it closes the sign-in tab it opened once you are signed in, and it may bring forward a claude.ai tab it opened itself. Of an Anthropic tab it opened, it learns only that the tab has begun loading a page, which the browser tells it without the page's address or content.

(g) Of (a) to (f), only your account name in (c) is sent to Licensor, in the approval check that section 10 describes; nothing else is. Section 10 describes the only things that may be.

7. NAMED DEPENDENCIES: THE OUTSIDE THINGS BEETHOVEN NEEDS

Beethoven works only while all of the following hold. None of them is within Licensor's control, and each is disclosed here, on the welcome page and where Beethoven is offered, so that you can decide with this in mind:

(a) your institution keeps your account, your access to its network (including any VPN it requires), its Open OnDemand portal with its shell, files and jobs features and, where used, its reverse proxy, and its computing systems; and its policies, firewalls, maintenance windows, queue rules and job limits allow what Beethoven does;

(b) Anthropic keeps offering Claude, Claude Code, its sign-in flow, the subscription plan you hold and Remote Control on terms that permit your use, keeps your plan eligible for Remote Control, and does not change, limit or enforce them against your account or your pattern of use;

(d) you keep your own accounts, do not share them, and keep your sign-ins current;

(e) the internet connections between your browser, your institution's systems and these services work.

10. WHAT LICENSOR RECEIVES, ACCESS RECORDS AND PRIVACY

(a) The approval check. Only after you have accepted this agreement, and only once your cluster has accepted your sign-in and your account name is known, the Extension asks Licensor's access service (https://beethoven-access.openspineconsortium.workers.dev) whether that account is approved: when you first sign in to your cluster after accepting this agreement, about once a day while it is in use, and again when you open the Extension's panel after a day has passed or after a no. Each check sends, over an encrypted connection and without cookies, your account name as your cluster confirmed it, your portal's hostname (on the ssh path, the hostname of the portal your institution's site profile names), the product name, the Extension's version, the installation identifier of section 3(e) and, as any request does, the time it was made. The service answers yes or no, and for a no may say that your account is bound to another installation, that this installation is bound to another account, or that the version is too old. Licensor's service keeps one record of the checks for each account and product: the account name, the product, the portal's hostname and the version of the latest check, when the account was first and last checked, how many checks there have been, the answer of the latest check and the reason given with a no, when the answer last changed, and a salted hash of the network address of the latest check (never the address itself); it also counts each day's checks per account and per hashed address, to limit them, and deletes those counts after two days. For each approved account it also records the installation identifier the account is bound to, with the product, the version and when that installation first and last asked, and for that installation the account it is bound to; and, when a check is refused because of another installation or another account, how many times and when the first and the last time were, with the first eight characters of a one-way hash of the refused installation's identifier. When another installation asks about your account, Licensor is told by e-mail, at most once a day per account, with a link that can move your approval to that installation. The Extension keeps a yes for up to a day, and for up to seven days when the service cannot be reached, so that an outage on Licensor's side does not stop your work; it keeps a no for ten minutes.

(b) Two files. Once a day, and only after you have accepted this agreement, the Extension also fetches from Licensor's website a small file naming the address of the access service (https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/services.json) and a signed list of withdrawn versions (https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/killlist.json). Those requests are sent without cookies and carry nothing about you beyond what any web request carries (your network address). The check in (a) and these two files are the only requests the Extension makes to Licensor.

(c) The Extension sends no error reports, no crash reports and no usage data, and there is no activation step: it has no code for them and no address to send them to. Your acceptance record (the version and hash of this text, the summary and the sentence shown, what you ticked, whether you opened the full text, the time, the install id, your account name once known, the software versions), your statements, your audit log, your settings, the key of section 5(b)(iii) and what the Extension remembers about your worker stay in your browser; Licensor does not receive them. The install id is the installation identifier of section 3(e), which the approval check in (a) sends, as it sends your account name.

(d) Access records. An access request on the request page records what you enter there: your account name, your name, your institutional e-mail, the Google account at which you are to receive the invitation to the private listing (Licensor adds it to the Google Group that may open that listing), what you will use Beethoven for and, if you attach one, your CV; and, when the service asks you to confirm your institutional mailbox, the time you confirmed it. Licensor's own records hold the approval and withdrawal decisions about your account, with the name and e-mail given and their dates, the installation your approval is bound to (section 3(e)) and the record of the approval checks described in (a). Licensor deletes a CV twelve months after deciding on the request (twelve months after the request, if no decision is made), or at once if it refuses the request or withdraws the approval, and keeps the other records for the life of your access and six years after, to prove the license and its terms.

(e) The full privacy statement is in PRIVACY.md, which forms part of this agreement.

11. NOT FOR CLINICAL OR HIGH-RISK USE, AND NOT FOR RESTRICTED DATA

Beethoven is a research and teaching tool. It is not a medical device and must not be used for diagnosis, treatment or any other clinical decision, or as a source of medical advice, or in any setting where its failure could cause injury, death or damage to property. Because of section 5(e), it must not be used on protected health information, FERPA-protected education records, data collected under an IRB protocol that has not approved this use, or export-controlled technical data.

17. UPDATES AND CHANGES TO THESE TERMS

Updates to the Extension are distributed through its private listing on the Chrome Web Store, and your browser installs them by itself. The Bridge you installed on your computer does not update itself: if a later version of the Extension needs a newer Bridge, the Extension says so and offers the newer installer from its own package, which you run as you ran the first. A Framework that an earlier version of the Extension installed in your own cluster account is never updated on its own, and the Extension no longer installs or updates one. Where your institution's lab keeps one shared copy of the Framework, the lab updates that copy, your next worker start uses it, and the Extension shows the version in use under Details. Each version ships the terms that apply to it. Licensor may change these terms for future versions. A change is never effective merely by being posted: Beethoven shows a changed agreement on its welcome page and asks you to accept it again, by the same steps, before the new version is used. A change to section 19 or 20 applies only to disputes that arise after you accept it. If you decline a changed agreement, you may keep using the version you accepted for as long as your approval and the evaluation period last, or stop using Beethoven; earlier acceptance records are kept.

18. EXPORT AND SANCTIONS

You must comply with the export-control and sanctions laws that apply to you. You represent that you are not located in, and will not use Beethoven in, a country or region subject to a comprehensive US embargo, and that you are not on a US government restricted-party list. The Extension contains cryptography to verify signatures and, for the ssh path, an ssh client that encrypts its connection to your cluster and makes and uses the key of section 5(b)(iii), all with your browser's own cryptography; the Bridge carries that connection and has no cryptography of its own; the Framework generates random per-job tokens and, in the one-time step of section 5(b)(v), has the cluster's own ssh-keygen make a key in your account.

19. DISPUTES: NOTICE FIRST, THEN INDIVIDUAL CLAIMS IN MICHIGAN COURTS

Please read this section; it affects how disputes between you and Licensor are resolved and is one of the terms named in the sentence you tick on the welcome page.

(a) Notice and 60 days to fix it, before any lawsuit. Before starting any lawsuit or other proceeding, the party with a claim sends the other a written notice, signed by that party personally, stating their name, the e-mail in the access record, the install id shown with the acceptance record on Beethoven's settings page, what the problem is and what outcome they want. Notice to Licensor goes to the notice address on the support page at https://openspineconsortium.com/beethoven/support.html; notice to you goes to the e-mail in your access record. The parties then have 60 days to resolve it in good faith, including one telephone or video call if either asks. Completing this paragraph is a condition of bringing any claim other than in small-claims court; a court may decide, at either party's request, whether it was completed. Any time limit that applies to the claim, including (e), is paused from the day the notice is sent until the 60 days end. Licensor owes you the same notice and the same 60 days.

(b) Where. Any lawsuit or proceeding arising out of or relating to Beethoven, your access or this agreement is brought only in the state courts sitting in Wayne County, Michigan, or the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan, and both parties consent to their jurisdiction, except that (1) either party may bring an individual claim that qualifies in the small-claims court of the county where you live, and (2) you may bring a claim where you live where the law of your state gives you that right and does not allow it to be waived.

(c) CLASS-ACTION WAIVER. YOU AND LICENSOR EACH AGREE TO BRING CLAIMS AGAINST THE OTHER ONLY IN AN INDIVIDUAL CAPACITY, AND NOT AS A PLAINTIFF OR CLASS MEMBER IN ANY PURPORTED CLASS, COLLECTIVE, CONSOLIDATED OR REPRESENTATIVE PROCEEDING. If a court holds this paragraph unenforceable for a particular claim, it is severed for that claim only and the rest of this agreement stands.

(d) Fees. Each party pays its own lawyers, except that in a proceeding other than small claims the court may award the prevailing party its reasonable attorney fees and costs; this does not displace any award a statute gives you.

(e) One year to bring contract and warranty claims. This paragraph does not apply to claims under a consumer-protection statute or to any claim whose period the law does not allow to be shortened.
